generation.hypothesis: Advanced processing routes that refine microstructure (e.g., via rapid solidification or additive manufacturing with optimized post-annealing) can improve the magnetocaloric performance of alloys by reducing magnetic hysteresis and enhancing the entropy change under moderate magnetic fields.
generation.material_initial_state: A conventionally processed magnetocaloric alloy (such as a La(Fe,Si)₁₃ or Gd-based alloy) exhibiting relatively coarse grains and irregular phase distribution.
generation.intervention: Apply advanced processing techniques to control the microstructure, specifically targeting finer and more uniform grain sizes along with a controlled distribution of magnetic phases.
generation.conditions: Operational temperature near room temperature and under moderate magnetic fields typical for cooling applications.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined microstructure with uniform grain size and well-aligned magnetic domains established by the optimized processing route.
generation.mechanism: The controlled microstructural architecture reduces energy losses due to magnetic hysteresis and improves the alignment of magnetic domains under an applied field, thereby increasing the isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature shift during the magnetocaloric cycle.
generation.predicted_outcome: The processed alloy is expected to exhibit enhanced cooling efficiency, evidenced by a larger isothermal entropy change and lower hysteresis losses compared to the same alloy produced via conventional processing.
generation.baseline: Magnetocaloric materials fabricated using traditional melting and casting techniques that result in larger, less controlled grain structures.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent on achieving a sufficiently controlled microstructure; adverse effects may occur if the processing parameters lead to unintended phase segregation or if the intrinsic magnetocaloric properties of the alloy are not optimal.
generation.uncertainty: The extent of the improvement in magnetocaloric properties and its scalability to industrial production require further systematic experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the advanced processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in hysteresis and an increase in isothermal entropy change compared to the conventionally processed samples, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Unlike other conventional alloys based on a “principal element,” high-entropy alloy (HEA) is a unique material that maintains a random solid solution structure without forming intermetallic compounds in operating temperatures due to its high configurational entropy [1] – [3] . It also has outstanding physical and chemical properties, which makes it a potential replacement for traditional metallic materials, and it has recently been referred to as a multi-principal element alloy (MPEA) or compositionally concentrated alloy (CCA) [4] – [9] .

As attention in HEAs increases, many studies have been conducted to explore its mechanical, physical and chemical properties [10] – [15] . In particular, equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, which was the first developed HEA, is the most studied because of its excellent combination of tensile strength and elongation along with excellent fracture toughness and corrosion resistance [6] , [16] – [21] . However, despite the advantages of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEA, many issues arise owing to its low yield strength and costly and complex thermomechanical processing (i.e., multiple casting → hot rolling → homogenization → cold rolling → annealing → cutting, etc.

For centuries, constructions with high mechanical requirements have been built using steel or iron-based alloys, while titanium or aluminum have been used for light-weight constructions. In gas turbines nickel- or cobalt-based superalloys are used because of their extremely good mechanical properties and oxidation resistance over long periods of time at high temperatures. The main properties of these alloys are given by their base element, while the addition of other elements in small amounts leads to fine adjustments of a specific behavior [ [1] ].

An unconventional approach of alloy design is based not on a main element, but on a chemical composition that exhibits a large number of elements with none of them dominating. In this group one differentiates between single-phase high entropy alloys (HEA) [ [2] ] and multiphase compositionally complex alloys (CCA). Multicomponent alloys were examined first by Yeh [ [2] ] and Cantor [ [3] ]. decision.trend: Earlier research on magnetocaloric materials began with well‐established systems like Gd‐based alloys and La(Fe,Si)₁₃ compounds, which offered large entropy changes but suffered from high magnetic field requirements and thermal hysteresis. Subsequent efforts—exemplified by Heusler alloys—focused on tuning magnetic transitions through compositional modifications. In parallel, studies on high-entropy alloys (as in PMC11375712) revealed that complex magnetic transitions and intrinsic magnetocrystalline anisotropies can be engineered, although these efforts have primarily focused on composition rather than the microstructural arrangements that govern domain behavior and hysteresis.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue is achieving a large isothermal entropy change and adiabatic temperature change near room temperature under moderate magnetic fields while simultaneously minimizing hysteresis losses. Up to now, most strategies have concentrated on compositional adjustments, leaving the role of microstructure less exploited in optimizing the magnetocaloric effect.
decision.lever: Advanced processing routes to tailor grain size and phase distribution (for example, using rapid solidification or additive manufacturing with optimized post-annealing) to achieve a controlled magnetic domain structure
decision.why: Optimizing the microstructure is a logical next step as it builds on past compositional tuning and leverages processing techniques to reduce hysteresis and enhance the field-induced entropy change. By controlling the microstructural features that dictate domain behavior and phase evolution, researchers can address the limitations of current materials under moderate magnetic fields and near room-temperature conditions.
